learning_objective: The learner will distinguish six kinds of factual error by choosing the kind that each of eight error reports describes, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** error-type-sorter
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** distinguish
**Learning Objective:** The learner will distinguish six kinds of factual error by choosing the kind that each of eight error reports describes, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Factual Error, The Accuracy Metric (both defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each report the learner chooses one of six kinds. A choice is correct when it matches the Correct kind column in Content. Mastery is at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the kind definitions is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) An outdated statement is a wrong fact. (2) A claim with no source is false. (3) A simplification is never an error. **Instructional Rationale:** Distinguishing kinds of error is an Analyze-level action, and the six kinds overlap in everyday speech. Eight reports that each isolate one kind make the learner attend to what exactly is wrong. **Content:** The six kinds: Wrong fact, Wrong number or unit, Misattributed quote, Outdated statement, Unsupported claim, Misleading simplification. The eight reports: | # | Report shown to the learner | Correct kind | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | A reading says the human heart has three chambers. | Wrong fact | The claim is false: the human heart has four chambers. | | 2 | A lab page tells students to measure 5 liters where its own source says 5 milliliters. | Wrong number or unit | The fact is right and the unit is wrong. | | 3 | A history page credits a famous speech to the wrong speaker. | Misattributed quote | A real statement is credited to the wrong person. | | 4 | A technology page tells students to use a program that was discontinued in 2019. | Outdated statement | The advice was sound when written and no longer works. | | 5 | A health page says studies prove a diet works and cites nothing. | Unsupported claim | No evidence is offered, so no one can tell whether it is true. | | 6 | A science page says plants get their food from the soil and never mentions sunlight. | Misleading simplification | It is partly true and leaves out what changes the meaning. | | 7 | A math page says the area of a rectangle is its length plus its width. | Wrong fact | The formula is false: area is length times width. | | 8 | A page quotes statistics from a recent study that is ten years old. | Outdated statement | The statistics were current once and are old now. | **Provenance:** The reports are illustrative cases written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The kinds follow the chapter section "Factual Error". The product named in report 4 is not named in the sim. **Rules:** Each report has exactly one correct kind. Reports 1 and 7 are Wrong fact, and reports 4 and 8 are Outdated statement. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads one report and sees the six kinds. 2. The learner may open the kind definitions. Opening them does not change the score. 3. The learner chooses a kind, and the choice is committed. 4. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text. 5. After report 8 the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 8 reports in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [kind]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [kind]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 8 correct on the first attempt". At 7 or more it adds "You can name the error." Below 7 it lists the Why text of each missed report. **Starting State:** The first report, the six kinds, and the definitions closed. The question shown is "What kind of error is this?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter lists six kinds of factual error: wrong fact, wrong number or unit, misattributed quote, outdated statement, unsupported claim, and misleading simplification.
